But Saturn V's upper stages were more powerful, so its total payload to the Moon was actually higher. SLS compensates by using the lighter Orion capsule instead of the heavier Apollo stack.

timeline.heading: HOW IMF LOANS ACTUALLY WORK
timeline.body: The IMF does not hand over a lump sum. It disburses in tranches, each unlocked by a review confirming the borrower met specific conditions. Miss a condition, lose the next tranche. This gives the Fund leverage — but only if it enforces.

timeline.heading: THE LETTER VS. THE SPIRIT
timeline.body: Conditions are written as measurable benchmarks: 'list state enterprises on the exchange.' A government can satisfy the letter — put names on a board — without satisfying the spirit — actually sell shares to private buyers. This gap between formal compliance and real reform is the oldest game in IMF politics.

timeline.heading: WHY EGYPT CANNOT SELL
timeline.body: The Egyptian military controls an estimated 25-40% of GDP through companies in cement, construction, food, and hospitality. Genuine privatization would require the military to surrender profitable assets. Every Egyptian government since Mubarak has promised reform and found reasons to delay.

timeline.heading: THE IMF'S DILEMMA
timeline.body: If the Fund rejects cosmetic compliance, it withholds funds from a country of 110 million people already in a currency crisis. If it accepts, it rewards the performance and undermines its own conditionality framework for every other borrower. Egypt has bet — repeatedly and correctly — that geopolitical importance buys tolerance.

timeline.heading: WHERE DRUGS ARE ACTUALLY MADE
timeline.body: About 87% of active pharmaceutical ingredients for the US market are manufactured abroad — primarily in India, China, and Ireland. India alone supplies over 40% of US generic finished doses. This dependency built up over 30 years as manufacturers chased lower production costs and looser environmental rules.

timeline.heading: SECTION 232
timeline.body: Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 lets the president impose tariffs on imports that threaten national security — without Congressional approval. It was designed for steel and oil during the Cold War. Its use for pharmaceuticals would be a novel legal theory, stretching 'national security' to mean 'domestic health supply.'

timeline.heading: WHY YOU CANNOT RESHORING DRUG MANUFACTURING QUICKLY
timeline.body: A pharmaceutical plant takes 3-5 years to build, validate, and receive FDA approval. Active ingredient synthesis requires specialized chemical engineering talent that the US has offshored for decades. Even with unlimited money, the labor and regulatory pipeline cannot be compressed below about 3 years.

timeline.heading: THE GENERIC MATH
timeline.body: Generic drugs are 90% of US prescriptions but only 18% of drug spending. Their margins are already razor-thin — often 2-5%. A 100% tariff on imported generics cannot be absorbed; it passes directly to patients or triggers shortages when manufacturers exit unprofitable products.

timeline.heading: THE GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: The Strait of Hormuz is 33 km wide at its narrowest, but the shipping lanes are just 3 km each — two one-way channels separated by a 3 km buffer. Roughly 21 million barrels of oil pass through daily, about 21% of global consumption.

timeline.heading: WHY PIPELINES DON'T ALREADY EXIST
timeline.body: They partly do. The UAE's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline (2012) can move 1.5 million barrels/day to a port on the Gulf of Oman, bypassing the strait entirely. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea handles another 5 million. But combined, these cover less than a third of the strait's throughput.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER ECONOMICS
timeline.body: Pipelines cost $1-3 per barrel to operate. Tankers through Hormuz cost around $0.50. In peacetime, the strait is simply cheaper — which is why bypass capacity stays underbuilt despite decades of threat.

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE SIGNAL
timeline.body: War risk premiums on tanker insurance are the market's real-time fear gauge for Hormuz. When premiums spike from 0.05% to 1-2% of cargo value, it adds $1-3 per barrel overnight — enough to flip the pipeline economics completely.

timeline.heading: THE ANOMALY
timeline.body: The Molucca Sea is the only place on Earth where two tectonic plates subduct toward each other simultaneously. The Philippine Sea Plate dives west while the Eurasian Plate dives east, with the Molucca Sea Plate being consumed from both sides. It is the last remnant of a vanishing ocean plate.

timeline.heading: MAGNITUDE VS ENERGY
timeline.body: The Richter scale is logarithmic in amplitude but exponential in energy. A 7.4 quake releases roughly 11 times more energy than a 6.4, and 1,000 times more than a 5.4. This is why the jump from 'felt it' to 'catastrophic' happens across just two magnitude points.

timeline.heading: HOW TSUNAMIS FORM
timeline.body: Only vertical seafloor displacement generates tsunamis. A strike-slip quake (plates sliding past each other) of the same magnitude typically does not. The fault geometry matters more than the number on the scale.

timeline.heading: THE SPEED PROBLEM
timeline.body: A tsunami crosses open ocean at 700-800 km/h — jet aircraft speed — but stands only 30-60 cm tall, invisible to ships. It slows to 30-50 km/h in shallow coastal water, where the energy compresses vertically into destructive wave heights. Coastal cities near the epicenter may have under 15 minutes.

timeline.heading: THE MECHANISM
timeline.body: Most signup forms send a confirmation email automatically — no authentication required. An attacker scripts thousands of signups using a target's email address. The target's inbox fills with legitimate confirmation emails from legitimate services, each one individually harmless.

timeline.heading: WHY IT WORKS
timeline.body: The emails are not spam in the traditional sense. They come from real companies, pass SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication, and contain genuine opt-in requests. Spam filters are designed to catch forgery and bulk sends from single senders — not a distributed flood of authentic one-off messages.

timeline.heading: THE REAL DANGER
timeline.body: Volume is the distraction, not the goal. Attackers use subscription bombing to bury a genuine security alert — a password reset, a bank login notification, a two-factor code — under hundreds of irrelevant emails. The target never sees the one message that matters.

timeline.heading: THE DEFENSE GAP
timeline.body: Rate limiting helps but is per-service. No single service knows that 400 other services also just emailed this address. There is no cross-platform protocol for detecting coordinated signup abuse — each form operator sees exactly one request.

timeline.heading: THE OLD BARRIER
timeline.body: Games are written against Win32 and DirectX — Microsoft's proprietary OS and graphics APIs. Running them on Linux required either a native port (expensive, rare) or Wine, which reimplements Win32 call-by-call. For years, Wine's DirectX translation was too slow and too incomplete for modern games.

timeline.heading: WHAT PROTON ACTUALLY DOES
timeline.body: Valve's Proton wraps Wine with DXVK, which translates DirectX 9/10/11 calls to Vulkan in real time. Vulkan runs natively on Linux. The trick is that GPU-side work is already platform-agnostic — the translation overhead is almost entirely on the CPU setup calls, which are a small fraction of frame time.

timeline.heading: THE STEAM DECK EFFECT
timeline.body: Valve shipped the Steam Deck (2022) running Arch Linux, not Windows. Every compatibility bug reported by millions of Deck owners feeds directly into Proton fixes. Hardware created the install base that justified the software investment — a bootstrapping problem solved by selling the hardware at near cost.

timeline.heading: THE 5% NUMBER IN CONTEXT
timeline.body: Desktop Linux hovered at 1-2% for two decades — a figure so stable it became a running joke. The jump to 5% on Steam is driven almost entirely by one product (Steam Deck) and one compatibility layer (Proton). It is a case study in how a single committed vendor can move a number that an entire open-source ecosystem could not.

timeline.heading: TWO PHILOSOPHIES
timeline.body: CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computing) packs hundreds of powerful instructions into the chip — one instruction might move a whole block of memory. RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computing) uses simple instructions that each execute in one clock cycle. Arm is RISC. IBM's Power and x86 are CISC. The bet is which approach wastes less energy per unit of useful work.

timeline.heading: WHY ARM WON MOBILE
timeline.body: Arm does not manufacture chips. It licenses designs. This meant any phone maker could customize an Arm core for their exact power budget. By 2012, virtually every smartphone on Earth ran Arm — not because it was fastest, but because it was most adaptable.

timeline.heading: THE ENTERPRISE BARRIER
timeline.body: Datacenters ran x86 for decades not because the chips were better, but because the software ecosystem assumed x86. Enterprise software is compiled, tested, and certified for a specific architecture. Switching CPUs means revalidating every binary — a cost measured in years, not dollars.

timeline.heading: WHAT CHANGED
timeline.body: Cloud computing broke the lock-in. When you rent compute by the hour, you do not care what chip runs underneath — the cloud provider abstracts it. AWS proved this with Graviton (custom Arm) in 2018: same workloads, 40% less energy. That made the enterprise Arm case economic, not just technical.

timeline.heading: IBM'S POSITION
timeline.body: IBM has built its own RISC chips (POWER) since 1990 and designed mainframe processors since the 1960s. It understands high-reliability computing at a level few companies match. The strategic question is whether IBM brings its reliability engineering to Arm, or brings Arm's energy economics to its enterprise clients — or both.

timeline.heading: THE CORE PROBLEM
timeline.body: Getting a therapeutic gene into the right cells is harder than designing the gene itself. DNA does not cross cell membranes on its own. You need a delivery vehicle — and viruses are evolution's answer to exactly this problem, perfected over billions of years.

timeline.heading: HOW VIRAL VECTORS WORK
timeline.body: Engineers gut a virus of its disease-causing genes and replace them with therapeutic cargo. The viral shell still knows how to enter cells and deliver its payload, but it can no longer replicate. The virus becomes a biological FedEx truck.

timeline.heading: THE TARGETING PROBLEM
timeline.body: Most viral vectors infect many cell types indiscriminately. AAV9, the workhorse of gene therapy, crosses the blood-brain barrier but also hits the liver heavily. If your therapy is meant for neurons, liver accumulation is not just wasteful — it can be toxic.

timeline.heading: WHAT CONDITIONAL LOGIC MEANS HERE
timeline.body: Classical gene therapy is always-on: if the vector enters a cell, the gene expresses. Conditional logic means the cargo includes a molecular IF statement — express only if the cell contains a specific marker. This is the difference between a drug that floods the body and one that activates only where needed.

timeline.heading: WHY RNA MATTERS
timeline.body: DNA-based vectors integrate into the genome permanently — powerful but irreversible. RNA-based payloads are transient by nature: they do their work and degrade. For therapies that need a temporary effect or a safety valve, RNA gives you an off-switch that DNA cannot.

timeline.heading: PLASTICS ARE FOSSIL FUELS
timeline.body: About 8-10% of global oil production becomes plastic, not fuel. The feedstock is naphtha — a light fraction from crude oil distillation that sits between gasoline and kerosene. When oil stops flowing, it is not just cars and heating that suffer.

timeline.heading: THE CRACKING STEP
timeline.body: Naphtha enters a steam cracker at 850°C and breaks into ethylene, propylene, and other building blocks in under a second. These monomers then polymerize into polyethylene (bags, bottles), polypropylene (packaging, car parts), and PVC (pipes, cables). Nearly everything plastic traces back to this one thermal process.

timeline.heading: THE GULF'S ROLE
timeline.body: Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar collectively produce roughly 15-20% of global petrochemicals. Their advantage is not just oil — it is cheap ethane from natural gas, which cracks more efficiently than naphtha. Hormuz disruptions hit both the naphtha flowing out and the finished polymers flowing to Asia.

timeline.heading: WHY SUBSTITUTION IS SLOW
timeline.body: Plastics are not one material — they are thousands of formulations tuned to specific tolerances. Medical-grade polypropylene for syringes cannot be swapped for a different polymer without years of recertification. Supply shocks do not just raise prices; they create hard shortages in sectors that cannot substitute.

timeline.heading: THE CONCENTRATION RISK
timeline.body: Global petrochemical capacity clusters around four zones: the US Gulf Coast, the Arabian Gulf, Northeast Asia, and Northwest Europe. A disruption in any one zone cannot be fully offset by the others because crackers run at 85-95% utilization. There is almost no spare capacity in the system.

timeline.heading: THE ORIGINAL ARMS RACE
timeline.body: In the early web, spammers wrote simple regex crawlers: find anything matching name@domain.tld and add it to a list. Site owners responded by writing 'name [at] domain [dot] tld' or encoding addresses as HTML entities. This worked because crawlers were pattern matchers with no understanding.

timeline.heading: WHY OBFUSCATION WORKED FOR 25 YEARS
timeline.body: Harvesting was a volume game — billions of pages, fractions of a cent per address. Spending compute to decode obfuscated emails was not worth it when millions of plaintext addresses existed elsewhere. Economics, not technology, protected obfuscated addresses.

timeline.heading: WHAT LLMS CHANGE
timeline.body: A language model does not match patterns — it understands intent. It reads 'john (at) example (dot) com' the same way a human does, because it learned from text written by humans who understood these conventions. Every obfuscation scheme that a human can decode, an LLM can decode, at crawler-scale cost.

timeline.heading: THE ASYMMETRY
timeline.body: Obfuscation is a one-shot defense: you choose a scheme and publish it. The attacker can test every scheme offline against a model before crawling. The defender cannot update deployed pages in response. This is a structurally losing position — the same asymmetry that doomed CAPTCHAs.

timeline.heading: WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS
timeline.body: Server-side approaches — rendering the address only after JavaScript execution, requiring authentication, or using contact forms that never expose the address — survive because they never put the email in the HTML. The principle: if it is in the source, assume it is readable.

timeline.heading: THE WHOLE POINT
timeline.body: End-to-end encryption means only the sender and recipient hold decryption keys. The server carries ciphertext it cannot read. If the server can derive your private key, you do not have end-to-end encryption — you have a trust-me promise with extra steps.

timeline.heading: WHAT A PRIVATE KEY IS
timeline.body: In asymmetric cryptography, your private key is a number only you possess. Your public key is derived from it mathematically. Anyone can encrypt a message with your public key; only your private key can decrypt it. The entire security model collapses if anyone else holds that number.

timeline.heading: SALT AND NONCE
timeline.body: A salt is random data mixed into key derivation so identical passwords produce different keys. A nonce (number used once) ensures the same plaintext encrypts differently each time. Hardcoding either one is a textbook failure — it means every user's key derivation follows the same path, making bulk decryption trivial.

timeline.heading: WHY THIS KEEPS HAPPENING
timeline.body: Building a messenger is easy. Building the cryptography correctly is extraordinarily hard. Signal's protocol took years of peer review. Apps that roll their own crypto or misuse primitives routinely ship encryption that looks real in a feature list but provides zero actual protection.

timeline.heading: THE AUDIT TEST
timeline.body: The single most important question about any encrypted messenger: has the cryptographic implementation been independently audited, and is the report public? If the answer is no, the encryption claim is unverified marketing.

timeline.heading: NOT JUST A PREFERENCE
timeline.body: Austrian neutrality is constitutional law, not foreign policy. The 1955 Federal Constitutional Law on Neutrality prohibits joining military alliances and forbids foreign military bases on Austrian soil. Violating it requires a two-thirds parliamentary supermajority — the same threshold as amending the constitution itself.

timeline.heading: THE DEAL
timeline.body: Austria's neutrality was the price of sovereignty. The Soviet Union agreed to withdraw occupation forces in 1955 only after Austria committed to permanent neutrality modeled on Switzerland. Without this guarantee, Austria would have been partitioned like Germany.

timeline.heading: WHAT PERMANENT MEANS
timeline.body: Five countries hold permanent neutral status recognized in international law: Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Finland, and Turkmenistan. Unlike situational neutrality (choosing not to fight in a specific war), permanent neutrality is a standing legal obligation that applies to all conflicts.

timeline.heading: THE AIRSPACE QUESTION
timeline.body: Overflight rights are not a technicality. Granting military overflight to a belligerent is an act of non-neutrality under the 1907 Hague Convention. Neutral states must deny transit to all belligerents equally — permitting one side's flights while blocking the other's would void the neutral status entirely.

timeline.heading: HOW RADAR SEES
timeline.body: Radar fires electromagnetic pulses and listens for reflections. A metal aircraft reflects strongly because free electrons in the metal oscillate with the incoming wave and re-radiate it. Stealth means either deflecting that reflection away from the receiver or converting it to heat before it bounces back.

timeline.heading: THE CLASSIC TRADE-OFF
timeline.body: Conventional radar-absorbing materials use carbon or iron particles suspended in polymer matrices. They absorb well in a narrow frequency band, but degrade above 300°C. Leading edges of supersonic aircraft exceed that easily — so the surfaces that need absorption most are the ones where coatings fail first.

timeline.heading: WHY GRAPHENE
timeline.body: Graphene is a single atom thick sheet of carbon with extraordinary electrical conductivity. When electromagnetic waves hit it, the free electrons dissipate the wave energy as heat across the lattice. The absorption bandwidth can be tuned by stacking layers or adjusting defects — something bulk materials cannot do.

timeline.heading: WHAT DECIBELS MEAN HERE
timeline.body: Radar absorption is measured in negative decibels: −10 dB means 90% absorbed, −20 dB means 99%, −60 dB means 99.9999%. Each −10 dB reduces the reflected signal by a factor of ten. At −60 dB, an aircraft's radar signature shrinks to roughly that of an insect.

timeline.heading: THE DIAMOND ROLE
timeline.body: Diamond has the highest thermal conductivity of any natural material — five times copper. In a composite, it acts as a heat sink: graphene converts radar energy to heat, diamond conducts that heat away before it damages the coating. The combination solves the thermal-vs-absorption trade-off that has limited stealth coatings for decades.

timeline.heading: THE TRANSPARENCY PARADOX
timeline.body: Every blockchain transaction is public and permanent. Pseudonymous addresses provide privacy, but the transaction graph — who sent what to whom — is visible to everyone. This makes cryptocurrency simultaneously the easiest financial system to use anonymously and the easiest to trace forensically.

timeline.heading: HOW ATTRIBUTION WORKS
timeline.body: Firms like Elliptic and Chainalysis maintain labeled databases of wallet addresses: known exchanges, mixers, sanctioned entities. When stolen funds move, analysts trace the chain of transfers and match patterns — timing, amounts, splitting behavior — against known laundering signatures.

timeline.heading: CROSS-CHAIN LAUNDERING
timeline.body: Stolen tokens are swapped across blockchains using bridges or decentralized exchanges to break the trail. Each hop adds noise, but also leaves a new set of on-chain footprints. The cat-and-mouse game is whether the attacker can reach a no-KYC off-ramp before analysts flag the funds.

timeline.heading: LAZARUS GROUP'S PATTERN
timeline.body: North Korea's Lazarus Group has a distinctive fingerprint: they target DeFi protocols with smart contract exploits, move funds through specific mixing services, and convert to stablecoins in characteristic batch sizes. This behavioral signature is now so well-documented that attribution often happens within hours of a theft.

timeline.heading: WHY NORTH KOREA
timeline.body: UN sanctions cut North Korea off from the global financial system. The regime generates hard currency through counterfeiting, arms sales, and — since 2017 — cryptocurrency theft. The UN Panel of Experts estimated DPRK cyber operations funded roughly 40% of the weapons program as of 2023.

The Strait of Hormuz narrows to 24 miles between Iran and Oman — roughly one-fifth of the world's daily oil supply passes through it, and the Asian refineries that supply most of Australia's fuel depend on crude shipped through this single chokepoint.
Geologists struck oil in Australia's Bass Strait, launching three decades of near self-sufficiency in crude that led policymakers to treat fuel security as someone else's problem.
Australia co-founded the International Energy Agency after the OPEC shock, pledging to hold 90 days of net oil imports in strategic reserve — a commitment it has not met in over a decade.
Iran and Iraq attacked over 400 oil tankers in the Persian Gulf during the Tanker War, establishing that Iran would weaponize commercial shipping lanes when it felt strategically cornered.
Bass Strait oil production fell below half its 1985 peak, tipping Australia into permanent net dependence on imported crude and refined fuel.
Four of Australia's eight oil refineries shut down as operators decided importing refined fuel from Singapore and South Korea was cheaper than processing crude domestically.
Trump withdrew from the Iran nuclear deal and reimposed sanctions, collapsing the diplomatic framework that had kept Tehran's threats to close Hormuz largely rhetorical.

BP Kwinana and ExxonMobil Altona closed in the same year, leaving Australia with just two operating refineries; the Morrison government offered emergency subsidies to prevent those last two from following.

Government data showed Australia holding roughly 50 days of fuel reserves — barely half the IEA's 90-day obligation — with diesel stocks so thin that a single disrupted shipping route could trigger shortages within weeks.

Over 80 percent of Australia's refined fuel was imported, most of it from refineries in Singapore, South Korea, and Japan that themselves depend on Middle Eastern crude shipped through the Strait of Hormuz.

timeline.heading: THE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: Hormuz is 21 nautical miles wide at its narrowest. Shipping lanes compress further — two 2-mile-wide channels separated by a 2-mile buffer. Every tanker leaving the Persian Gulf must pass through this corridor.

timeline.heading: THE VOLUME
timeline.body: About 20% of the world's daily oil consumption transits Hormuz. No pipeline network can substitute this volume — Saudi east-west pipelines max out at roughly a quarter of Gulf seaborne exports.

timeline.heading: WHY IT CANNOT BE BYPASSED
timeline.body: The UAE built the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline specifically to skirt Hormuz, but it handles only 1.5 million barrels per day. Gulf states collectively export over 17 million by sea. Geography is the constraint: the Gulf has exactly one exit.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Iran and Iraq attacked each other's oil tankers from 1984 to 1988. Over 400 ships were hit. The US eventually intervened with naval escorts (Operation Earnest Will), but insurance rates and oil prices spiked long before military action resolved anything.

timeline.heading: THE TOLL IDEA
timeline.body: Iran has floated Hormuz toll schemes since the 1990s, arguing sovereign rights over its territorial waters on the strait's northern shore. International law (UNCLOS Article 38) guarantees transit passage through straits used for international navigation — toll or no toll, blocking transit violates it.

timeline.heading: WHAT BIOCHAR IS
timeline.body: Wood or crop waste heated above 300°C in a low-oxygen kiln. The process (pyrolysis) drives off volatile gases and leaves a porous carbon skeleton that resists microbial breakdown for centuries.

timeline.heading: WHY IT HOLDS NUTRIENTS
timeline.body: Biochar's surface area is enormous — a single gram can exceed 300 square meters. Cation exchange sites on that surface grab ammonium, potassium, and calcium ions from soil water and release them slowly to roots. Synthetic fertilizer, by contrast, dissolves fast and leaches.

timeline.heading: THE N2O CONNECTION
timeline.body: Soil bacteria convert surplus nitrogen fertilizer into nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas 273 times more potent than CO2 over 20 years. Biochar adsorbs excess nitrogen before bacteria can process it, which is why N2O emissions drop.

timeline.heading: THE PERMANENCE QUESTION
timeline.body: Ordinary compost decomposes within years, returning its carbon to the atmosphere. Biochar's aromatic carbon rings are thermodynamically stable — radiocarbon dating of charcoal in Amazonian terra preta soils shows persistence exceeding 2,000 years.

timeline.heading: THE TILLAGE LINK
timeline.body: Plowing exposes buried organic matter to oxygen, accelerating decomposition. No-till farming preserves soil carbon but often requires more herbicides. Biochar offers a third path: it maintains soil structure and water infiltration without mechanical disturbance.

timeline.heading: WHY ALTITUDE MATTERS
timeline.body: Satellites at the same altitude travel at the same orbital speed. A collision between two objects in the same shell produces fragments that stay in that shell for years. Different altitudes mean different speeds, so encounters are brief and rare.

timeline.heading: KESSLER SYNDROME
timeline.body: In 1978, NASA scientist Donald Kessler showed that above a critical density, collisions produce enough fragments to trigger further collisions in a chain reaction. The debris belt becomes self-sustaining. No technology exists to clean a Kessler cascade once it starts.

timeline.heading: THE FCC'S UNLIKELY ROLE
timeline.body: The FCC regulates satellite orbits not because of space law but because of radio spectrum. Every satellite transmits, so the FCC claims jurisdiction over orbital parameters through its spectrum licensing authority. There is no dedicated US orbital traffic regulator.

timeline.heading: THE MANEUVER BURDEN
timeline.body: LEO satellites already perform hundreds of collision-avoidance maneuvers per year. Each burn consumes finite propellant and shortens satellite lifespan. As constellations grow from hundreds to tens of thousands of satellites, the maneuver rate scales faster than linearly.

timeline.heading: THE DECAY TRADEOFF
timeline.body: Lower orbits have more atmospheric drag, so debris re-enters and burns up within a few years. Higher orbits are cleaner for operations but debris persists for decades. Mega-constellations deliberately choose low altitudes so failed satellites deorbit naturally — but that concentrates traffic in a narrow band.

timeline.heading: THE PRINCIPLE
timeline.body: The US Constitution places all military authority under civilian command. The President is Commander-in-Chief; the Secretary of Defense is a civilian by law (any recently retired officer must receive a congressional waiver). The principle predates the republic — it was a direct response to Cromwell's military rule in England.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE CHIEF OF STAFF ACTUALLY DOES
timeline.body: The Army Chief of Staff does not command troops in combat — that authority runs through the combatant commanders to the Secretary of Defense. The Chief of Staff trains, equips, and organizes the force. It is an administrative role with enormous influence but no operational command.

timeline.heading: THE SENATE CONFIRMATION QUESTION
timeline.body: Service chiefs are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate for fixed terms (typically 4 years). Fixed terms exist precisely to insulate military leadership from political pressure. Firing a confirmed chief is legal but historically extraordinary — it signals that the insulation failed.

timeline.heading: THE TRUMAN PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Truman fired General MacArthur in 1951 for publicly contradicting Korea policy. It was deeply unpopular — MacArthur's approval rating was higher than Truman's — but it established that civilian supremacy means the President's strategic judgment overrides a general's, even a famous one's.
